rows.selection_reason: With zero completed experiments, there is no evidence to exploit, so the priority is establishing a maximally informative baseline. Config_001 (rna_only, singleprofile, pca_n2000) is the simplest, most robust configuration in the space: it uses a standard linear dimensionality reduction (PCA-2000), a single profile, and no aggregation or fusion, minimizing the number of confounded design choices. This gives a clean RNA-only performance floor that will serve as the reference point for every subsequent experiment—allowing us to isolate the marginal contribution of multiprofile aggregation, alternative RNA encoders (scvi, scgpt), image modality, and multimodal fusion. Without this anchor, any multimodal or multiprofile result would be difficult to interpret because we would not know how much of the performance comes from each design axis. It is the single most informative first experiment under a limited budget.

Evidence: Only one experiment is complete (config_001: rna_only, singleprofile, pca_n2000 → acc 0.485, F1 0.464), giving a single unimodal RNA baseline with no information about image utility, fusion, or multiprofile effects. Question: Does adding the image modality (resnet50) to the RNA-only model improve validation accuracy? This is the core hypothesis of a multimodal cellular profiling study. config_016 (multimodal, singleprofile, pca_n2000, resnet50, concat) is the most direct and minimal extension of config_001—it holds the RNA encoder, profile setting, and fusion strategy constant while introducing only the image branch with the simplest fusion (concat). This isolates the effect of adding image information with minimal confounding. Why best next: With a limited budget, establishing whether multimodal > unimodal is the highest-value uncertainty to resolve. A clear improvement over 0.485 would justify investing further in multimodal configurations (better encoders, multiprofile, transformer aggregation); a null or negative result would redirect the search toward optimizing the unimodal model or questioning the image pipeline. No other single experiment reduces this central uncertainty as directly.

Evidence: config_016 (multimodal, singleprofile, pca_n2000, resnet50, concat) achieved 0.527 acc / 0.510 F1, a clear +4.2% improvement over the rna_only baseline (config_001, 0.485 acc). This confirms that adding the image modality is beneficial. Question: Does moving from singleprofile to multiprofile (with avgpool aggregation) further improve performance while keeping the same RNA encoder, image encoder, and fusion strategy? This is a direct, single-axis extension of the best configuration so far. Rationale: With only two experiments completed, the largest unexplored design axis is profile setting (single vs. multi). Multiprofile captures richer temporal/dynamic information and could yield a gain comparable to the modality addition. config_018 isolates this change cleanly (only profile_setting and aggregation differ from config_016), making attribution straightforward. If multiprofile helps, it opens the aggregation-strategy sub-axis (avgpool vs. transformer) for further exploitation; if it does not, we can confidently redirect budget toward fusion strategy or alternative encoders. This is the highest-information-per-experiment choice under the limited budget.

Evidence: config_018 (multimodal, multiprofile, pca_n2000, resnet50, avgpool, concat) is the current best at 0.619 acc, showing that multiprofile + avgpool aggregation is the dominant design choice (+0.092 over singleprofile). However, we have only tested one aggregation method (avgpool) for multiprofile. Question: config_020 isolates the aggregation method (transformer vs avgpool) while holding all other variables constant relative to config_018, directly testing whether a more expressive, attention-based aggregation can better capture inter-profile relationships than simple averaging. Why this is the best next experiment: Aggregation is the mechanism by which the largest observed gain (multiprofile) is realized, so understanding its ceiling is critical. A single-variable change from the current best keeps the comparison clean and maximally informative. If transformer significantly outperforms avgpool, it opens a high-impact direction for subsequent experiments; if not, we can confidently rule out transformer aggregation and redirect budget toward fusion strategy or image encoder upgrades.

Evidence: config_018 (multimodal, multiprofile, pca_n2000, resnet50, avgpool, concat) is the current best at 0.619 acc / 0.610 F1, showing that multiprofile + avgpool + multimodal is a strong combination. However, fusion strategy has only been tested as 'concat' across all experiments; we have no evidence about whether learned weighted fusion could better balance the RNA and image contributions. Question: Does weighted fusion outperform simple concatenation in the multimodal, multiprofile, avgpool setting? This is a single-variable change from the current best, making it a clean exploitation experiment. Rationale: Under limited budget, testing fusion is the lowest-risk, highest-information next step because (a) it directly extends the best configuration, (b) it isolates one architectural decision, and (c) the result informs whether weighted fusion should be carried forward when we later explore stronger image encoders (ViT-L) or RNA encoders (scvi/scgpt). If weighted fusion helps, we gain an immediate improvement and a better template; if not, we confirm concat suffices and avoid wasting future experiments on weighted variants.

Evidence: The best configuration so far (config_019, acc=0.639) uses PCA n2000 as the RNA encoder with multiprofile, ResNet50, avgpool, and weighted fusion. All completed experiments used PCA n2000, so the RNA encoder axis is completely unexplored. Question: Does a learned single-cell RNA encoder (scvi_n200) improve over linear PCA when all other settings are held at their empirically best values? This is a clean, single-variable comparison (PCA vs. scvi) that isolates the contribution of learned RNA representation. Why this is the best next experiment: The RNA encoder is a fundamental design axis—PCA is a simple linear projection while scvi learns a nonlinear latent representation tailored to single-cell data. If scvi improves performance, it opens a productive direction (configs 031-039) and suggests further investment in learned encoders. If it does not, it confirms PCA sufficiency and redirects budget toward the image encoder axis (ViT-L) or other factors. This maximizes information gain per experiment under the limited budget.

Evidence: The current best (config_031, acc=0.678) uses scvi_n200 + resnet50 + avgpool + weighted. All multimodal experiments so far have used resnet50 as the image encoder, leaving the image-encoder choice (resnet50 vs. imagenet_vit_l) completely unexplored. This is a high-impact design axis because ViT-L is a substantially more powerful, architecture-distinct image encoder. Question: Does upgrading the image encoder to imagenet_vit_l improve performance when combined with the already-optimized RNA encoder (scvi_n200), multiprofile, avgpool, and weighted fusion? Why this is the best next experiment: It is a clean single-variable change from the current best, isolating the image-encoder effect. A positive result would identify a new promising direction; a null or negative result would let us rule out ViT-L across all remaining configurations, saving multiple future experiments under the limited budget. The other untested axes (transformer aggregation, concat fusion) have weaker priors for improvement given the consistent avgpool>transformer and weighted>concat trends observed with PCA, making them lower-information choices.

Evidence: The current best (config_037, acc 0.706) uses scvi_n200 + imagenet_vit_l + avgpool + weighted. The only prior aggregation comparison (config_018 avgpool 0.619 vs config_020 transformer 0.579) was done with the weaker pca_n2000 + resnet50 setup, so it is unclear whether avgpool's advantage persists or reverses with richer SCVI and ViT-L representations. Question tested: Does transformer aggregation interact favorably with the stronger encoders (scvi_n200 + imagenet_vit_l), potentially outperforming avgpool? Why this is the best next experiment: It is a single-variable change from the current best, directly exploiting the promising direction while resolving a key uncertainty about the aggregation choice at the top of the performance hierarchy. The result will either confirm avgpool as the robust choice (solidifying the design) or reveal that transformer unlocks additional gains with richer features—both outcomes are highly informative for subsequent experiments under a tight budget.

The current best (config_039: scvi_n200, imagenet_vit_l, transformer, weighted, 0.725) has established that multimodal + multiprofile + weighted fusion + transformer aggregation + imagenet_vit_l is the strongest configuration family. The one major untested variable in this family is the RNA encoder: we've shown scvi_n200 > pca_n2000 (~4% gain), but scgpt has never been tested in any multimodal setting. Config_051 (scgpt, imagenet_vit_l, transformer, weighted) is a clean A/B test against config_039, isolating the RNA encoder as the only changed variable. This is the highest-uncertainty, highest-impact remaining design decision: if scgpt outperforms scvi_n200, we get a new best; if not, we confirm scvi_n200 as the superior encoder and can redirect remaining budget to other refinements. Under a limited budget, resolving this single binary question in the context of the current best configuration is more informative than testing lower-priority variants (e.g., concat fusion, which has consistently underperformed weighted).

The current best configuration (config_039: scvi_n200, imagenet_vit_l, transformer, weighted) achieves 0.725 acc / 0.685 F1. Prior evidence shows weighted fusion outperforms concat with pca_n2000+resnet50 (config_019: 0.639 vs config_018: 0.619), but this gap was only ~2% and in a lower-performance regime. Config_038 is a single-variable change (weighted→concat) from the best config, directly testing whether the weighted-fusion advantage persists when combined with transformer aggregation and the stronger ViT-L image encoder. If concat performs comparably, it confirms the design is robust and simplifies the search; if weighted is clearly superior, it validates the current best and narrows the design space. Under a limited budget, this targeted exploitation of the most promising region is more informative than exploring a new axis (e.g., scgpt, which config_051 showed to be poor) or a less-connected variant.
